title: Nurse-driven daily sedation interruption: a lean redesign of the morning process to raise completed interruptions
subtitle: Value stream mapping, gemba walks and A3 cycles in a 16-bed intensive care unit
statement: A 16-bed intensive care unit uses a nurse-driven daily sedation interruption protocol, but in the last three months the safety screen was documented on 71 percent of eligible patient-days, the interruption on 38 percent and the paired breathing trial on 29 percent. The gap lies after the screen. The unit wants to use lean methods to find where the morning process breaks down and to raise completed interruptions to 70 percent of eligible patient-days within six months, without more self-extubations or distress.
whoAffected: Ventilated adults on continuous sedation, their families, bedside nurses, respiratory therapists and the physicians who lead morning rounds.
whatHurts: Missed interruptions prolong sedation and ventilation; nurses feel the decision to stop sedation as a personal risk; families at the bedside may be distressed by awakening.
currentPractice: A written protocol with a safety screen at the start of the day shift; interruptions and breathing trials scheduled separately; reasons for not proceeding recorded as free text.
whyNow: A two-year-old protocol with low adherence, a sponsor agreement from the medical director and nurse manager, and a lean facilitator from November 2026.
constraints: No additional staff; changes must fit the existing morning workflow before 09:00 rounds; the hospital lean facilitator is available four hours a week from November 2026 to April 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Every eligible patient has sedation stopped safely each morning so that they wake, breathe on their own and leave the ventilator as early as they can.
summary: Problem framed as a lean redesign of the morning sedation interruption process.
